body:
# Partial Yao-Yao partitions: exact possibilities and obstructions

This audit separates literal closed convex parts with a common affine
fiber core from partitions that allocate the positive mass on their
boundaries. The distinction is material for mixed-integer measure.

## 1. A closed convex part containing a fiber flat is cylindrical

Let F={z_0} x R^d and let Q be a nonempty closed convex subset of
R^(n+d) containing F. Then Q is invariant under every translation
parallel to F. In particular Q=D x R^d for a closed convex D subset R^n.

Proof. Fix w in Q and a vector v=(0,v_c) parallel to F. Choose f in F.
For every 0<epsilon<1 the point

    (1-epsilon)w+epsilon(f+v/epsilon)

belongs to Q, by convexity and containment of F. As epsilon tends to
zero it converges to w+v, which belongs to Q by closedness. Applying
the same argument to -v proves translation invariance. The claimed
product representation and closedness of D follow by intersecting Q
with R^n x {0}.

Therefore oblique cuts cannot occur in a partition of the ambient space
into closed convex regions all containing the whole fiber flat F.
Every separating hyperplane between such regions has zero continuous
component in its normal.

There is a corresponding bounded-body statement. Suppose two convex
parts of a convex body have disjoint nonempty ambient interiors and
both contain an actual full-dimensional fiber {z_0} x C_(z_0).
A separating hyperplane for their interiors contains their common
fiber. Since the affine hull of that fiber is F, the hyperplane's
continuous normal component is zero. Thus weakening the common core
to an entire actual full-dimensional fiber still forbids an oblique
separating interface between those parts.

## 2. Exact equipartition by literal closed parts fails with core mass

Let mu be the mixed-integer or intrinsic measure, normalized or not.
Suppose r>=2 closed parts Q_1,...,Q_r cover S and all contain its
z_0-fiber, of positive mass w_0. Then

    sum_i mu(S intersect Q_i)>=mu(S)+(r-1)w_0>mu(S).

The central fiber is counted r times and every other point at least
once. In particular all parts cannot have mass mu(S)/r.

An explicit example works for every n>=1 and d>=0: take

    C=[-1/4,1/4]^n x K,

where K is a d-dimensional convex body (a point when d=0). Then
S={0} x K. Any closed regions with common core {0} x R^d each contain
all of S, so every part has the full mass. This is not an issue that
can be removed by asserting that ordinary hyperplane boundaries have
zero measure: the common integer fiber carries all the relevant mass.

## 3. A valid exact two-part allocation for one integer variable

Now let n=1 and q>=1. Let S=C intersect (Z x R^d), measured by H_q,
and let M=H_q(S)>0. For each integer z write w_z=H_q({z} x C_z).
Choose an integer weighted median z_0 with w_(z_0)>0, so that

    L=sum_(z<z_0)w_z<=M/2,
    R=sum_(z>z_0)w_z<=M/2.

Such a z_0 exists by taking an index where the cumulative positive
weight first reaches M/2. Set w_0=w_(z_0) and

    a=M/2-L.

Then 0<=a<=w_0. The fiber C_(z_0) has affine dimension q. Choose a
linear functional b on continuous coordinates that is nonconstant on
this affine hull. Its hyperplane sections are H_q-null. The continuous
cumulative q-volume of C_(z_0) along b takes every value between zero
and w_0, so choose t with

    H_q({x in C_(z_0):b dot x<=t})=a.

Define actual subsets of C by

    A_-=(C intersect {z<z_0})
          union ({z_0} x {x in C_(z_0):b dot x<=t}),

    A_+=(C intersect {z>z_0})
          union ({z_0} x {x in C_(z_0):b dot x>=t}).

Each set is convex. A segment between two points on the boundary fiber
stays in its convex half-fiber; a segment with at least one point on
the strict integer-coordinate side remains strictly on that side except
possibly at its endpoint, and stays in C by convexity. They cover C,
and their intersection is the q-null slice z=z_0, b dot x=t. Therefore

    H_q(S intersect A_-)=L+a=M/2,
    H_q(S intersect A_+)=R+w_0-a=M/2.

This is an exact equipartition into two convex actual sets. In general
the sets are not closed. Their common set is a cut of the actual fiber,
not the entire fiber flat. If z_0 is in the interior of the integer
projection, their closures can overlap on the whole central fiber,
reintroducing positive double-counted mass. Thus closing the sets is
not harmless.

For q=0 the analogous exact allocation need not exist, because the
measure has atoms. A singleton cannot be divided into two disjoint
measurable sets of half its counting measure. Fractional allocation
would be a different object, not the asserted actual-set partition.

## 4. A discontinuity obstruction to an ordinary Borsuk-Ulam selection

For -1/2<=s<=1/2 define the convex trapezoid in R x R

    C_s={(z,x):0<=z<=1,
                  |x|<=[(1+s)(1-z)+(1-s)z]/2}.

It is a convex body and depends continuously on s. Its only integer
fibers are z=0 and z=1, of lengths 1+s and 1-s, with total mass two.
For s>0 the only integer weighted median is z_0=0: at z=1 the mass
strictly to the left is 1+s>1. For s<0 the only integer weighted median
is z_0=1. At s=0 both indices are allowed.

There is no continuous selection of a permissible integer median apex
through this family. A continuous map from the connected parameter
interval into the discrete set {0,1} is constant, whereas its values
are forced to differ on the two sides of zero. Hence a direct
Borsuk-Ulam construction cannot simply assume a continuously selected
integer apex. A set-valued or combinatorial replacement would need
its own proof; no such replacement is asserted here.

## 5. Which halfspace orientations a partial partition can control

For a nonempty cylindrical region Q=D x R^d, every ambient hyperplane

    a dot z+b dot x=c,  b!=0,

meets Q and has points of Q on both strict sides: fix any z in D and
move x arbitrarily far in the two b directions. Thus a collection of
such regions has no Yao-Yao avoidance property for halfspaces with
nonzero continuous normal component. Only the purely integer normal
family can be controlled by its projected cone geometry alone.

This remains visible inside bounded product bodies. For example take
C=[-1,1] x [-1,1] and use the two pieces of Section 3 at z_0=0 with
b=1,t=0. The hyperplane x=0 meets the ambient interiors of both pieces,
and both pieces have positive mixed-integer mass on both sides. Neither
the equipartition nor convexity by itself certifies a containing
halfspace's required fraction at a single point of the common slice.

Consequently the valid two-part allocation supplies exact part masses,
but no all-orientation Grunbaum guarantee. Any mixed-integer use must
add a quantitative argument for oblique and continuous-normal caps,
track the allocated boundary-fiber mass, and justify the integer-center
selection. This file proves none of those missing assertions by analogy
with the ordinary continuous Yao-Yao theorem.
